title: Verb + wh-clause
subtitle: That might explain why he's unhappy.
summary: Follow verbs with a wh-clause: add an object where the verb demands one, choose between whether and if, and use the way and as to correctly.

lesson.heading: Verb + wh-clause
lesson.text: Many verbs can be followed by a clause beginning with how, what, when, where, which, who or why. Also: arrange, calculate, check, choose, debate, determine, discover, discuss, establish, find out, forget, guess, imagine, know, learn, notice, plan, realise, remember, say, see, talk about, think (about), understand, wonder.

examples.text: I couldn't decide **which train to catch**.
Let's consider **how we can solve** the problem.

lesson.heading: wh-word + to-infinitive
lesson.text: Most of these verbs also allow a wh-word (but not *why*) + to-infinitive. As soon as we put a subject into the wh-clause, the to-infinitive is impossible.

examples.text: Did you find out **where to go**?
I can't imagine **what he likes** about jazz.
I decided **that I ought to leave**.
examples.note: many of these verbs also take a that-clause

lesson.heading: Verbs that need an object first
lesson.text: Some verbs must have an object before the wh-clause. Also: advise, inform, instruct, remind, teach, tell, warn. **ask** and **show** often have an object, but not always.

examples.text: She reminded **me** what (I had) to do.
I told **Linda** how to get to my house.
I asked (**him**) how I could get to the station, and he told me.
She taught **me** how to play chess.

lesson.heading: the way instead of how
lesson.text: We can often use **the way** rather than *how* to talk about a route or a means of doing something. But never put the two together.

examples.text: Go back **the way** (that / by which) you came.
examples.note: informally: Go back how you came.

examples.text: Have you noticed **the way** (that / in which) he spins the ball?
They showed me **the way to get** to the track.
examples.wrong: the way how to get to the track

left.label: whether
left.text: Used as a wh-word to show possible choices - and the only choice before a to-infinitive. Also after choose, consider, debate, determine, discuss, know (in questions and negatives), think about, wonder.
examples: He couldn't remember **whether** he had turned the computer off.
You have 14 days to decide **whether to keep** it or not.
I wondered **whether to retrace** my steps.

right.label: if
right.text: Has a similar meaning to *whether* in a finite clause, but is never used before a to-infinitive.
examples: He couldn't remember **if** he had turned the computer off.
not ~~to decide if to keep it or not~~
*ask, conclude, explain, imagine, realise, speculate and think are not used with whether + to-infinitive at all.*

lesson.heading: whether-clause or that-clause?
lesson.text: The two are not interchangeable. A **whether**-clause leaves the question open; a **that**-clause states something as a fact.

examples.text: I didn't know **whether** the shop was shut.
examples.note: = if the shop was shut or not

examples.text: I didn't know **that** the shop was shut.
examples.note: suggests the shop was in fact shut

lesson.heading: as to (formal)
lesson.text: In formal contexts, especially writing, **as to** can come before a wh-clause with a meaning like *about* or *concerning*. It is most common before *whether*.

examples.text: Opinion was divided **as to whether** the findings from the study were representative.
There was some discussion **as to whether** the snow would arrive.

lesson.text: Before a to-infinitive, use *whether*, never *if*: *decide whether to keep it*, not ~~decide if to keep it~~.

exercises.prompt: Match each beginning with the wh-clause that completes it.

pairs.left: Before the meeting finished they arranged
I saw Sarah leave the building, but I didn't notice
When I saw Hugo alone at the party I wondered
After I'd dismantled the motor I couldn't remember
pairs.right: how to fit the parts back together.

pairs.left: To win a prize you had to guess
pairs.right: how many sweets were in the jar.

exercises.prompt: Anna was new in the office and I had to keep reminding ___ everyone was.
exercises.explanation: remind must have an object before the wh-clause: reminding her who everyone was.

exercises.prompt: As the guests came in Diego told ___ to put their coats.
exercises.explanation: tell needs an object, and the wh-word can then be followed by a to-infinitive.

exercises.prompt: She was ___ whether to invite Jeremy over for dinner.
exercises.explanation: debate takes whether + to-infinitive; think does not (only think about does), and explain never does.

exercises.prompt: I have to ___ whether to get a job or apply to go to college.
exercises.explanation: Only 'talking or thinking about choices' verbs like choose take whether + to-infinitive.

exercises.statement: When the snow started falling it was very light, and I couldn't decide if to carry on or go back down.
exercises.explanation: ... I couldn't decide whether to carry on or go back down. if is never used before a to-infinitive.

exercises.prompt: There was some discussion through the day as ___ whether the snow would arrive before my descent.
exercises.explanation: The formal linker is as to + wh-clause, most often as to whether.

exercises.statement: In the morning they showed me the way how to get to the track up the mountain.
exercises.explanation: ... showed me the way to get to the track. (or ... showed me how to get to the track.) We never use the way how.

exercises.prompt: Which verbs can be followed by whether + to-infinitive?
As the snow got heavier I began to realise ___ my life was in danger.
exercises.explanation: He was becoming sure of a fact, so a that-clause is right; whether would leave the question open.

exercises.prompt: I knew there was a shepherd's hut on this side of the mountain, but I didn't know ___ it was nearby or miles away.
exercises.explanation: Two open possibilities are being weighed, so we need whether (or if), not that.

exercises.prompt: Put this formal sentence in order.
exercises.answer: Opinion was divided as to whether the findings were representative
exercises.explanation: as to introduces the topic of the question in formal writing.
